title: Disagreeing with Brookmeyer on soloists and improvisation
summary: He disagrees that an arrangement can be jazz without improvisation; the chart is only a vehicle for soloists.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Okay. There’s a phrase the I heard from Dave Rivello, who said —

Said he heard it from Maria Schneider, who heard it from Bob Brookmeyer, okay? I’m tracing the lineage. And the statement was, from Brookmeyer, you should try to hold off as long as you can in an arrangement before you pass it to a soloist. So my question is do you agree with that, and the follow-up is have you ever felt like you want to give soloists some guidance for the way they’re going to solo on this chart that you’ve spent many hours working on?

Just the opposite. As a matter of fact I don’t agree with Bobby. Bobby at one point made the statement that a jazz arrangement could be jazz without improvisation. The creative art of manipulating notes in a jazz style was enough without improvisation. To me the chart is just a vehicle. It’s just a skeleton to get the improvisation out there. So my focus is the jazz improvisation. And like for instance when I wrote for — the very first album I had, Bud Shank on alto and Clay Jenkins on trumpet and I did a Horace Silver tune. Now in some way I guess I did do what you’re asking about knowing that Bud Shank did not play in that same style as Clay Jenkins. I kept the alto solo changes to be very comparable to the style of bebop and post-bop that Bud Shank would play. And then, when I transitioned to the trumpet solo I went into the Coltrane modal changes that I knew that would be very comfortable for Clay. I guess in a way I did guide it there, but my real focus is I’m there for the soloist. That’s the whole idea of the chart. If you listen to all my arrangements it is about the soloist, especially with my brothers.
Yes, the one I was listening to last night, I think it was Clay playing on it. And he had a lot of space, as did the tenor player who followed him.
